Orchot Tzadikim 5:35: And let this rule always remain in your hand: a person should not fill his every craving with eating and drinking, but should eat and drink to keep his body sound, and should withhold his hand even from what is permitted. And a person should not love the world in order to eat and drink and enjoy it. And so one of the sages said: I eat in order to live. And the fool said: I live in order to eat. And of this it is said (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul, but the belly of the wicked shall want."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:36: And likewise, one who marries a wife should think of it for the sake of Heaven, that he fulfill the commandment of being fruitful and multiplying, and have offspring who serve the Blessed Lord and fear Heaven. Or he should think that he thereby satisfies his desire and spends his passion with his own wife, so that he not crave other women. Or in order to be intimate with his wife when he knows she desires him, so that she not crave other men. Or he should intend it for the health of his body, since the emission of seed is beneficial to the health of the body; but whoever engages in relations excessively will bring many illnesses upon himself.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:37: And whoever walks along this path is, all his days, entirely a servant of the Blessed Lord — even at the time he conducts business, and even at the time of marital relations, because his intent in everything is only to obtain his needs, so that his body remain whole in order to serve the Blessed Lord. And even at the time he sleeps, if he sleeps so that his soul may rest and his body rest so that he not fall ill — since he cannot serve the Blessed Lord while ill — then his sleep too becomes service of the Blessed Omnipresent. Of this matter our Sages commanded and said (Avot 2:12): let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven. And this is what Solomon said in his wisdom (Proverbs 3:6), "in all your ways know Him, and He will straighten your paths."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:38: A person should abandon all these [lesser] loves and cling to love of the Blessed Creator, as it is written (Deuteronomy 6:5), "and you shall love the Lord your God." And love of the Blessed Lord is the ultimate purpose of all qualities and the end of all virtues in the ranks of all people of divine service, and all traits are like a ladder to the level of love; and it is the free gift of soul of the pious, the prophets, and the ascetics, and there is nothing higher than its final attainment.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:39: And many times the [sacred] text places the fear of God before love of Him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 10:12), "and now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but to fear the Lord your God and to love Him." And because love is the ultimate purpose and the end of asceticism, and the level closest to the level of love of God — it is impossible for a person to attain it except after his fear and dread of God have preceded it. And therefore fear was placed before love.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:40: And what is this love? It is the soul's love and its inclination of itself toward the Blessed Creator, so that it cling to His supernal light. This soul is the source of understanding, and it is pure and clear; and the Creator binds it to the body, whose desire is great, in order to test whether it will walk in the ways of the Lord. And because a person is clothed in a body created with an animalistic spirit, the soul created from God has no power to think of its Creator, since it is intermingled with the desires of the body. And throughout a person's childhood, he seeks and asks for nothing but his own desires and pleasures. Because of the great desires of the body — eating and drinking and the delicacies of this world, which is a world of vanity and falsehood — and because he thinks of gathering great wealth, the soul has no power to think of the Blessed Creator, for it is clothed in vain vanities. But once the soul senses what benefit there is for itself apart from partnership with the body, it will then long to seek rest from the traits of the body, as a sick person longs for a physician. And when the soul is healed of its ailments, it will have its own light and its own strength. And behold, the soul is full of love, and that love is bound up with joy, and that joy drives away from his heart the pleasantness of the body and the delight of the world. And that joy grows fierce and overpowers his heart, and all the pleasures in the world are as nothing compared to the surging strength of the joy of love of the Blessed Lord, and all the delights of his own children are as though they never existed, compared to the delight of a heart that loves the Lord with all its heart.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:41: And all his thought is on how to do the will of the Blessed Creator, and to bring merit to the many, and to sanctify the Name, and to give himself over in love of the Lord. And this is the fear of the Lord: that he not transgress what is written in the Torah — the love, such as Pinchas, who gave himself over in love of the Lord; and Abraham our father, who said (Genesis 14:22-23), "I have raised my hand to the Lord, God Most High, Maker of heaven and earth, that I will not take so much as a thread or a shoelace"; and Elisha, who did not wish to take anything from Naaman (2 Kings 5:15-16).
Orchot Tzadikim 5:42: And he should not neglect the study of Torah for the sake of the delight and pleasure of his own children, or the pleasure of gazing at women or conversing with them; and he should also give up outings with them; and he should sweeten his voice in song in order to fill his heart with joy in love of the Lord.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:43: Whoever serves out of love occupies himself with Torah and commandments, and walks in the paths of wisdom that show how to perform all the commandments out of love, and how to love the Blessed Lord with a great love — not because of anything in the world, not out of fear of evil, and not in order to receive the good; rather, he does the truth because it is the truth, and the good will come to him in the end. And this level is a very great level indeed, and not every person merits it, and it is the level of Abraham our father, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, called "My beloved" (Isaiah 41:8), because he served only out of love. And it is this that the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded through Moses our teacher, peace upon him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 6:5), "and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might." And when a person loves the Blessed Lord with the love that is fitting, he will at once perform all the commandments out of love.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:44: And what is this love? That he love the Lord with a very great and abundant love, until his soul is bound up in love of the Blessed Lord. And whoever constantly muses upon it is found to be, as it were, sick with the sickness of love, whose mind is never free of love for that woman, and he muses upon her constantly — whether sitting or standing, whether eating or drinking — even more than this shall be the love of the Lord in the hearts of those who love Him. And this is what Solomon said, by way of parable (Song of Songs 2:5), "for I am sick with love." And the whole Song of Songs is a parable for this very matter.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:45: It is a known and clear thing that love of the Holy One, blessed be He, is not bound to a person's heart until he muses upon it constantly as is fitting, and abandons everything else in the world but it, as it is said (Deuteronomy 6:5), "with all your heart and with all your soul." Therefore a person must understand and gain insight through the wisdom and understanding that make known to him his Maker, according to whatever capacity a person has to understand and attain.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:46: It is a commandment to love and to fear the glorious and awesome God, as it is said (Deuteronomy 6:5), "and you shall love the Lord your God"; and it is said (ibid. 6:13), "you shall fear the Lord your God." And this is the path to attaining love of the Blessed Lord: when a person contemplates His works and His wondrous, great creations, and sees from them His wisdom, which has no measure and no end, he will at once love the Blessed Omnipresent, and praise and glorify Him, and desire greatly to know the great Name — as David said (Psalms 42:3), "my soul thirsts for God, for the living God." And when one reflects on these things that David said, he is at once drawn backward and will fear and dread, and know that he is a small, lowly, and dim creature, standing with slight and meager understanding before the One of perfect knowledge; as David said (ibid. 8:4), "when I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers," and adjacent to it, "what is man, that You are mindful of him?" (ibid. verse 5).
Orchot Tzadikim 5:47: And when a person contemplates these great matters, and recognizes His greatness [as it exceeds] even an angel or a celestial sphere, and sees the wisdom of the Holy One, blessed be He, in all creatures and all creations, he adds love for the Blessed Omnipresent, and his soul thirsts and his flesh yearns to love the Blessed Omnipresent, and he will fear and dread his own lowliness, poverty, and insignificance when he compares himself to one of the holy bodies that the Blessed Lord created.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:48: And elsewhere it is said (Job 1:1), "and one who fears God," and they explained that this means one who fears the judgment of Heaven's punishment and of Gehinnom, and the punishments of this world (Sotah 27b). And this trait is very, very far from love. But one should fear the Blessed Lord as a man who loves his wife and she loves him, and he fears to do anything against her lest he lose her love — so is this matter: he strikes sparks of fire of love for the exalted Creator, and fears to transgress His commandments lest he forfeit love of the Blessed Creator.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:49: And this is "serve the Lord with fear" (Psalms 2:11) — this is the fear that comes from love — "and rejoice with trembling" — out of the greatness of your dread of the Creator, you shall rejoice to do His will.
Orchot Tzadikim 5:50: And this fear is the fear that comes from love, and of it is said (Isaiah 33:6), "the fear of the Lord is His treasure."
Orchot Tzadikim 5:51: And this love does not endure except in one who sets his mind to fulfill all the commandments according to their law, for whoever does not know the commandments which the Maker of all commanded him is not called a complete "lover." Therefore let him love everything that will bring him to love of the Blessed Creator, blessed be His Name. And whoever does this — it is good for him in this world and in the World to Come.
Orchot Tzadikim 6:2: Hatred. In this trait there is a negative commandment, as it is written (Leviticus 19:17), "you shall not hate your brother in your heart," and by this we were warned to remove the trait of hatred from our souls. And it is a trait that causes many sins, like slander. For whoever hates his fellow is always speaking of his hatred and complaining about him, and constantly seeks evil against him and rejoices at his misfortune; and it causes damages, for he will harm him whenever he is able to harm him, and he takes vengeance and bears a grudge against him, and will not show him mercy even if he is in great distress. And because of his hatred he will disparage the other's good deeds, and make them hateful in his own eyes and in the eyes of others; and he withholds good from its rightful owner, and will not admit the truth about him. And if he owes him money, he presses him harshly for it.
Orchot Tzadikim 6:3: There are several kinds of hatred. There is one who hates his fellow because he harmed him financially, or struck him, or shamed him, or gave him a bad name. Regarding these and the like of them, one should not hate his fellow and remain silent, as is said of the wicked (2 Samuel 13:22), "and Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon." Rather, it is a commandment to inform him and say to him: why did you do such-and-such to me? — as it is said (Leviticus, ibid.), "you shall surely rebuke your fellow." And if the offender then turns and asks his forgiveness, one must forgive him and not be cruel in forgiving; and even if he does not ask forgiveness, one should not hate him, but should conduct himself with him in love, and in the end this will bring the offender to correct what he has done wrong.
Orchot Tzadikim 6:4: There is a hatred worse than this, and it is baseless hatred, and it destroyed the Second Temple (Yoma 9b). And hatred that stems from envy is worse still, and a person ought to discipline his soul to keep far from these. And there is one who hates his fellow because he does not repay him with kindness, if he does not give him a gift as he wishes, or does not lend to him in his time of need — all this a person ought to keep far from. Rather, he should accept out of love whatever the Blessed Creator decrees for him, and not trust in man; and he should think: had I merited it from the Blessed Omnipresent, He would have given it to me apart from the gift or the loan of flesh and blood. And if he stands in poverty and distress, or is ill and afflicted with sufferings, he should think that the Creator has decreed all this upon him for his own good, to be accepted out of love. And there is no doubt: by doing this, all hatred will depart from his heart. And this is a great foundation and a strong pillar for Torah and commandments — to accept everything out of love.
Orchot Tzadikim 6:5: And he should accustom himself to this, and say of all that befalls him, "this too is for the good." And by intending this in his heart, and rejoicing in the judgment of the Blessed Creator, he will be saved from hatred, enmity, and envy.
Orchot Tzadikim 6:6: And likewise a craftsman who hates his fellow craftsmen — all this is vanity and great evil, for he should think: no person can earn more than what the Creator has decreed for him.
Orchot Tzadikim 6:7: And the worst and harshest of the kinds of hatred is such as people who hate those who rebuke them, and those who discipline them to teach them the straight path, as the matter is said (Amos 5:10), "they hate him who reproves in the gate." And there is a hatred worse than this: such as people who hate those who do good and pursue righteousness, as the matter is said (Psalms 38:21), "they are my adversaries because I follow after good." And those who walk this path hate the Lord, for they hate those who love Him, and they hate the Torah and the commandments, since they loathe, despise, and hate those who fulfill it.
Orchot Tzadikim 6:8: The wise man said: if you wish your friend to hate you, visit him constantly; and if you wish him to love you, visit him only at long intervals. And of this it is said (Proverbs 25:17), "let your foot rarely be in your neighbor's house, lest he grow weary of you and hate you."
Orchot Tzadikim 6:9: And you must know that whoever hates people, they too will hate him; and whoever increases hatred in his heart brings evil upon himself. And when there is love that is not for the sake of Heaven, it will turn into great hatred and envy, as is said of Amnon (2 Samuel 13:15), "and Amnon hated her with a very great hatred."
Orchot Tzadikim 6:10: Do not trust the counsel of one who hates you and is your enemy, as it is said (Proverbs 27:6), "but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful (profuse)." And know that many people show love in their words, yet may be complete haters in their hearts, and you must not trust them, as it is said (ibid. 26:24), "he who hates disguises it with his lips, but he lays up deceit within him." And even though his tongue flatters you and speaks softly, do not incline your heart toward him, as it is said (ibid. verse 25), "when he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for there are seven abominations in his heart." And this is like what Joab showed Abner son of Ner (2 Samuel 3:27), and Amasa son of Yeter (ibid. 20:9-10) — peace and love — until he killed them. And like Ishmael with Gedaliah son of Achikam (Jeremiah 41:1-2), until he killed him. One of the sages said: the best thing you can do, of all you may think regarding your enemy, is to turn him back to your love, if you are able.
Orchot Tzadikim 6:11: There is a hatred that is a commandment, such as toward a wicked person who does not accept rebuke, as it is said (Proverbs 8:13), "the fear of the Lord is to hate evil"; and it says (Psalms 139:21-22), "do I not hate those who hate You, O Lord, and do I not strive with those who rise up against You? I hate them with the utmost hatred; they have become enemies to me." And one should hate falsehood and lying words. In sum: one should hate everything that distances him and keeps him from love of the Maker of all, as the matter is said (ibid. 119:128), "I hate every false way." And this is a great principle: that a person hate every falsehood. And whatever hatred he adds toward the ways of falsehood, he adds love for the Torah, as it is written (ibid. 119:163), "I hate and abhor falsehood, but I love Your Torah." And he should love truth and peace, as it is written (Zechariah 8:19), "and love truth and peace."
Orchot Tzadikim 7:2: Mercy. This trait is very praiseworthy, and it is one of the thirteen attributes ascribed to the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written (Exodus 34:6), "merciful and gracious." And whatever a person is able to practice of it, he should practice and strive for. And just as a person wishes to be shown mercy in his own time of need, so it is fitting for him to show mercy to whoever is in need, as the verse says (Leviticus 19:18), "and you shall love your fellow as yourself."
Orchot Tzadikim 7:3: The Blessed Creator apportioned this trait to the righteous and to His servants, that they be recognized by it, as you know of Joseph (Genesis 43:30), "for his compassion was stirred." And it is fitting for the intelligent man that the trait of mercy and graciousness be fixed and present in his heart at all times.
Orchot Tzadikim 7:4: And there are several kinds of compassion, far apart from one another. A father's compassion for his son is a compassion that comes from the nature common to all living creatures, in the manner of dogs and beasts. And if he withholds the rod of discipline from his son because his compassion is stirred against striking him, and lets him go according to the wantonness of his own evil heart — behold, this compassion drives out and destroys the son from the life of the World to Come. Behold, a master shows compassion to his servant, and a person shows compassion to his fellow when he hopes for some benefit from him — in all such cases it is very good for him to take hold of the trait of compassion in his heart. But the good and superior kind of compassion is that he show compassion to his son by bringing him to the service of the Blessed Creator, as it is written (Isaiah 38:19), "the father shall make known Your truth to the children." And he should have compassion for his son's soul more than for his body, and he must strike him with the rod of discipline, guiding him in the straight path even with severity, for this severity is itself compassion. And even one who raises an orphan, of whom it is said (Exodus 22:21), "you shall not afflict any widow or orphan" — it is a commandment to discipline him in order to guide him to the straight path. Nonetheless one must lead the orphan with more compassion than any other person, only not letting him go according to the wantonness of his own heart.
Orchot Tzadikim 7:5: And one must also not show too much compassion to himself, but must discipline himself and subdue his evil inclination.
Orchot Tzadikim 7:6: And likewise he should show compassion to his poor relatives, as it is written (Isaiah 58:7), "and do not hide yourself from your own flesh."
Orchot Tzadikim 7:7: And he should also show compassion to the poor, and especially to those who fear the Lord; and this is the essence of true compassion — showing favor and mercy to those who serve the Lord and do His will.
Orchot Tzadikim 7:8: But there is a compassion that is worse than cruelty: such as showing compassion to the wicked and supporting them. And there is a great stumbling-block for a man who raises up the wicked and lends them a hand, while lowering the good and rejecting them. Of this it is said in the Torah (Deuteronomy 13:9), "your eye shall not pity him, nor shall you spare him." One should not show compassion to a poor man in judgment, as it is written (Exodus 23:3), "nor shall you favor a poor man in his lawsuit" — so as not to bend justice on account of the poor man's distress. And there is a compassion that is actually cruelty: such as one who gives charity to a poor man, and afterward burdens that poor man, saying: I gave you such-and-such, you must now toil for me and serve me in return for all I have done for you. Of this it is said (Proverbs 12:10), "but the mercies of the wicked are cruel."
Orchot Tzadikim 7:9: One must also show compassion to animals, for it is forbidden to cause pain to living creatures, and of this the Torah said (Deuteronomy 22:4), "you shall surely help him lift it up again." And one must feed his animal before he eats himself (Berachot 40a).
Orchot Tzadikim 7:10: The trait of compassion is a sign of the seed of Abraham our father, the seed of Israel, as it is written (Deuteronomy 13:18), "and He will show you mercy, and have compassion upon you, and multiply you" (Yevamot 79a). Therefore every person should accustom himself to speak all his words in a tone of supplication and compassion; also at the time he prays, he should make his prayer one of supplication (Avot 3:13). And a person receives great reward for words of compassion, by speaking gentle words to the heart of a poor man.
Orchot Tzadikim 7:11: And many know the commandment obligating charity and the reward for its performance, but do not know the greatness of the commandment of [kind] words. Behold, our Sages said (Bava Batra 9b): whoever gives a coin to a poor man is blessed with six blessings, but whoever comforts him with words is blessed with eleven blessings. Therefore, with the speech of his lips, let him clothe the poor man in charity by speaking to his heart, and let his words be gentle to the poor and needy, and let him comfort him regarding his labors and the toil of his hands, and lift him up.
Orchot Tzadikim 7:12: And you, O son of man, show compassion to your own soul, which endures forever, so as to bring it to a wondrous delight that no eye has seen. And do not let the abundance of your desire bring you to sin, so that you be cast out from light into darkness. Have pity on yourself, and show mercy to your own soul, and do not desecrate the glory of your soul with the vanities of pleasures. The wise man said: from generosity of spirit, a person comes to stand firm in the trait of mercy. And in the words of Solomon, mercy and grace are commanded, in his saying (Proverbs 24:11), "deliver those drawn to death, and hold back those staggering toward slaughter."
